title: When Police Can Impound Your Motorbike in Vietnam: Licence, Papers and Alcohol
meta_description: Understand when Vietnamese traffic police can impound a rental motorbike: missing licence, papers and alcohol rules, the fines involved, and how to get the bike released.
h1: When Can Police Impound Your Rental Motorbike in Vietnam?
body_markdown:
Renting a motorbike in Hanoi gives you enormous freedom, but it also puts a Vietnamese-registered vehicle in your hands that does not belong to you. If traffic police stop you and find a problem with your licence, your paperwork or your alcohol level, they can have the motorbike impounded by police in Vietnam on the spot. Knowing when that can happen, and what to do afterwards, saves you hours of stress and a difficult conversation with the rental shop.

## Why impoundment matters for renters

As a renter you face two separate problems when a bike is seized. The first is practical: you are standing at the roadside without transport, and you need to understand the procedure, keep your documents safe and avoid signing anything you do not understand. The second is contractual: the vehicle belongs to the rental company, and most rental agreements hold the rider responsible for whatever happens during the rental period. Before you even pick up the keys, it is worth reading our overview of [rental documents and contracts in Hanoi](/en/topics/documents-and-contracts/) and keeping the [pickup checklist](/en/checklist/) at hand.

## What "tạm giữ" actually means

The Vietnamese term for police impoundment is "tạm giữ phương tiện" – the temporary seizure of a vehicle. Under Article 48 of Decree 168/2024/NĐ-CP, traffic police may hold a vehicle before the penalty decision is even issued, based on points b.1, 2 and 8 of Article 125 of the 2012 Law on Handling Administrative Violations ([Thư viện pháp luật](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/phap-luat/ho-tro-phap-luat/cac-loi-vi-pham-bi-tam-giu-xe-may-2025-theo-nghi-dinh-1682024-the-nao-su-dung-giay-phep-lai-xe-het--195961.html)). In practice, the bike is taken to a police storage compound and released only once the violation has been processed. The full text of the decree is published by the government's policy journal ([Toàn văn Nghị định 168/2024/NĐ-CP](https://xaydungchinhsach.chinhphu.vn/toan-van-nghi-dinh-168-2024-nd-cp-quy-dinh-xu-phat-vi-pham-hanh-chinh-ve-trat-tu-atgt-duong-bo-119241231164556785.htm)).

Impoundment is a preventive measure, not a punishment in itself. The logic is simple: if a rider has just committed a serious violation, letting them ride on would defeat the purpose of the stop. For you as a renter, the important consequence is time. A seized rental bike is not something you can simply walk away from, because the shop will want its vehicle back and will look at the contract to decide who bears the consequences.

## The most common trigger: riding without a valid licence

The single most common reason foreign riders lose a rental bike is a licence that is not valid in Vietnam. Your home licence on its own is not enough, and an International Driving Permit only works if it covers the exact vehicle class you are riding. We explain both points in detail in [foreign driving licences](/en/guides/foreign-driving-licence/) and [International Driving Permits for motorbikes](/en/guides/international-driving-permit-motorbike/).

Riding without any licence at all is treated as a serious violation. Under point a of clause 5, Article 18 of Decree 168/2024/NĐ-CP, riding a two-wheeler with an engine of up to 125 cm³ (or an electric motor of up to eleven kilowatts) without a licence carries a fine of between 2 and 4 million VND; for machines above 125 cm³, point b of clause 7 sets the range at 6 to 8 million VND ([Thư viện pháp luật](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/phap-luat/ho-tro-phap-luat/cac-loi-vi-pham-bi-tam-giu-xe-may-2025-theo-nghi-dinh-1682024-the-nao-su-dung-giay-phep-lai-xe-het--195961.html)). Licence violations of this kind appear on the list in Article 48 that justifies holding the vehicle ([Thư viện pháp luật](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/phap-luat/ho-tro-phap-luat/cac-loi-vi-pham-bi-tam-giu-xe-may-2025-theo-nghi-dinh-1682024-the-nao-su-dung-giay-phep-lai-xe-het--195961.html)). A rider who cannot produce a licence is therefore exposed twice: to a substantial fine and to losing the bike for the duration of the procedure.

Note that the legal framework was recently reformed. Decree 238/2026/NĐ-CP, in force since 15 August 2026, amended several articles of Decree 168 – but the provisions on licences and vehicle seizure (Articles 18 and 48) were not among the amended articles ([Thư viện pháp luật](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/chinh-sach-phap-luat-moi/vn/ho-tro-phap-luat/chinh-sach-moi/116118/toan-van-nghi-dinh-238-2026-nd-cp-sua-nghi-dinh-168-xu-phat-giao-thong-duong-bo)).

## Alcohol and other violations that lead to impoundment

Alcohol at the handlebar is treated harshly in Vietnam, and drink-driving offences are among the violations that can justify seizing the vehicle under Article 48 ([Thư viện pháp luật](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/phap-luat/ho-tro-phap-luat/cac-loi-vi-pham-bi-tam-giu-xe-may-2025-theo-nghi-dinh-1682024-the-nao-su-dung-giay-phep-lai-xe-het--195961.html)). The thresholds and the way testing works are a topic of their own, which we cover in [drink-driving rules for motorbike riders](/en/guides/vietnam-drink-driving-rules-for-motorbike-riders/). The practical rule for renters is simpler than any legal table: if you plan to ride, do not drink at all.

Beyond licences and alcohol, Article 48 lists a long catalogue of traffic violations in which holding the vehicle is permitted, drawn from the offence articles of Decree 168, including Article 18 on licences ([Thư viện pháp luật](https://thuvienphapluat.vn/phap-luat/ho-tro-phap-luat/cac-loi-vi-pham-bi-tam-giu-xe-may-2025-theo-nghi-dinh-1682024-the-nao-su-dung-giay-phep-lai-xe-het--195961.html)). You do not need to memorise the catalogue. The pattern to remember is this: the more serious the violation and the less able you are to lawfully continue riding, the more likely the police are to take the bike into custody instead of letting you ride on.

## What happens during and after the stop

When police wave you over, stay calm and cooperative. Take off your helmet, switch off the engine and hand over the documents they ask for. Ask for the penalty decision in writing, note the name and unit of the officers, and above all call the rental shop immediately: the bike is registered in their name, and experienced shops know exactly how the local procedure works. Our guide to [traffic police stops with a rental bike](/en/guides/traffic-police-stop-rental-bike/) walks through this moment in detail.

Do not hand over your passport as collateral and do not pay cash at the roadside without paperwork. Official fines in Vietnam are paid through the treasury or a bank, and the payment process is documented – see [how to pay a traffic fine in Vietnam](/en/guides/how-to-pay-a-traffic-fine-in-vietnam/). If your violation was recorded by a camera rather than a live stop, the notice can arrive later through the rental shop, as explained in [traffic-camera fines for rental motorbikes](/en/guides/traffic-camera-fine-rental-motorbike-vietnam/).

## Getting the bike released

A seized vehicle stays in police custody until the violation has been fully processed and the fine has been paid. Because the bike is registered to the rental company, the shop usually has to be involved in the release: the decision may name the vehicle owner, and the shop may need to send a representative or authorise one. In general terms, release requires a completed penalty decision, proof that the fine was paid, and proper identification of whoever collects the vehicle.

Procedures vary between districts and provinces, so treat any step-by-step description you read online – including this one – as a general picture. The authoritative instructions are written in the penalty decision itself, and following them exactly is the fastest way to get the bike back.

## Who pays: renter or rental shop

The seizure itself is a police matter, but the costs and consequences are a contract matter. Most rental agreements make the rider responsible for fines and for any complications that arise during the rental period, and shops commonly reserve the right to use the deposit to cover unpaid fines. Before you ride, ask two questions: who officially pays a fine issued to the vehicle, and who do you call if the bike is seized. A serious answer to both questions is a good sign; a shrug is a warning.

Keep every piece of paper connected to the case: the penalty decision, the payment receipt, the names and times you were given. If the shop deducts anything from your deposit, documented papers are the only thing that turns an argument into a straightforward refund discussion. The starting point for these clauses is our hub on [documents and contracts](/en/topics/documents-and-contracts/).

## How to avoid the situation altogether

Almost every impoundment of a rental bike traces back to one of three fixable causes. Fix them before you ride and the topic becomes theoretical.

- Sort out your licence first: an International Driving Permit with the right class, or a Vietnamese licence, carried every single time you ride.

- Carry the vehicle papers with you. The registration card belongs to the shop, but a copy should travel with the bike – see [papers to carry when riding](/en/guides/papers-to-carry-registration-card/).

- Treat alcohol and riding as mutually exclusive for the length of your trip.

None of this is complicated, which is precisely the point. A rider with a valid licence, the right papers and an empty glass is very unlikely to ever see the inside of a police storage compound – and far more likely to enjoy the ride that brought them to Hanoi in the first place.

editorial_notes: Đối chiếu trực tiếp ngày 16/10/2026: (1) danh sách vi phạm bị tạm giữ xe theo Điều 48 NĐ 168/2024/NĐ-CP — trích từ bài Thư viện pháp luật (URL 195961), đã mở và đọc; (2) toàn văn NĐ 168 trên xaydungchinhsach.chinhphu.vn (URL 2, chỉ để khai báo nguồn chính thức); (3) toàn văn NĐ 238/2026/NĐ-CP (URL 3): có hiệu lực 15/8/2026, KHÔNG sửa Điều 18 và Điều 48 — mức phạt nêu trong bài vẫn theo NĐ 168. Mức phạt đã nêu: Điều 18 khoản 5 điểm a = 2–4 triệu đồng (xe máy ≤125cm³ hoặc ≤11kW), khoản 7 điểm b = 6–8 triệu đồng (>125cm³). Bài KHÔNG nêu giá thuê xe, KHÔNG nêu ngưỡng nồng độ cồn cụ thể (đã dẫn link bài chuyên về luật nồng độ cồn thay vì nêu số liệu), KHÔNG phát minh thủ tục giải chấp — chỉ mô tả các bước ở mức tổng quát và hướng độc giả làm theo văn bản quyết định xử phạt. Biên tập viên nên xác minh lại mức phạt và tình trạng hiệu lực văn bản trước khi xuất bản.
